records.our_prose: In the interior valleys kale is a cool-season crop grown from fall through spring. Sow or set transplants in late summer (around August into September) for a fall and winter harvest, and again in February for a spring crop before the heat. Harvest the outer leaves cut-and-come-again; the leaves are sweetest through the cool, sometimes frosty winter. The hot Central Valley summer is left out of the calendar, since heat makes the leaves bitter and pushes plants to bolt. Keep moisture even and give afternoon shade at the warm shoulders.

records.our_prose: On the Florida peninsula kale is a cool-season crop. UF/IFAS lists the planting window from about September into February in central Florida and September into January in the far south, with harvest peaking December through February. Pick the outer leaves cut-and-come-again; the cool, frost-free-to-light-frost winter gives the best quality, and a rare frost only sweetens the leaves. The hot, humid summer, roughly May into September, is the off-season, when only tropical crops thrive. Watch for caterpillars and aphids in the warm shoulders.

records.our_prose: In the Arizona low desert kale is a cool-season crop planted as the extreme summer heat eases. University of Arizona guidance puts the planting window from about September through December, with October ideal once the weather cools, and the harvest from December into April. Pick the outer leaves cut-and-come-again through the mild, sometimes frosty winter. The long, intensely hot summer, roughly May through September, is the off-season. Keep moisture steady and shade young plants set out in early fall.

records.our_prose: You can sow kale seeds right in the garden or start them indoors. For spring, start seeds about a month before planting out, and set plants in the garden a few weeks before your last frost, or just sow seeds once the soil can be worked. For a fall crop, sow in mid to late summer so it is ready before winter. If you grow your own transplants, let them get used to the outdoors over a week before planting.

records.our_prose: Kale can be direct sown or transplanted. For a spring crop, start seeds indoors about 4 to 5 weeks before set-out and transplant around 4 to 5 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow as soon as the soil is workable; kale tolerates frost. For a fall and overwintering crop, sow in midsummer (often direct in the garden) so plants size up before cold, then harvest through fall and, in milder zones, winter. Harden transplants off over 7 to 10 days.

records.our_prose: A single kale plant yields a steady run of outer leaves over a long season rather than one harvest, roughly 0.5 to 1 pound or more per plant depending on variety, season length, and how often you crop it. Extension yields run about 5 to 10 pounds per 10 feet of row.
records.source_context: Kale Plant Productivity Plant 5-10 feet of kale per person for fresh use and an additional 15-20 for processing. Expect 3-5 pounds per 10 feet of row. Kale Nutrition Facts Kale has no fat, is high in vitamin A and vitamin C, is a good source of calcium and iron and is considered one of the most nutritious of vegetables.
